newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Opposition urges U.N. to act on Nigeria rights.
newsitem.headline: Opposition urges U.N. to act on Nigeria rights.

text.p: The leading Nigerian opposition group has urged the United Nations ahead of the annual session of the U.N. Human Rights Commission to speed up efforts to resolve Nigeria's "crisis".

NADECO (National Democratic Coalition), in a six-page letter sent to the commission, said Nigeria's 100 million people who live under military rule deserved a better situation concerning rights and democracy than they currently faced.

"Nigeria needs a healthy climate of human rights where basic freedoms are enjoyed, including the right of free political association, form political parties to contest elections and choose our leaders freely and democratically," it said. The document was made available to Reuters in Lagos on Friday.
The U.N. Human Rights Commission begins its session on Monday in Geneva where Nigeria is expected to be in dock for rights abuses.

"The U.N. needs to speed up to solve Nigeria's lingering crisis...We urge you to adopt the same yardstick in evaluating our transition process as you will in normal civilised democratic societies," the NADECO letter said.

A two-man U.N. mission sent to investigate human rights situation in Nigeria and report back before start of the Geneva meeting called off their visit last week after the military government refused them access to jails and detainees.
A three-man African team on a similar mission was due to arrive Lagos on Friday night at the invitation of the military authorities.

Local rights activists have condemned the African team's visit, saying it lacked objectivity and that the government wanted to use it counter whatever the U.N. mission would have written about Nigeria.

"We will paint the actual picture when the African team meets all rights groups on Saturday morning in Lagos," Clement Nwankwo, executive director of a leading rights group, the Constitutional Rights Project, told Reuters.

The African team, to be led by Ghanaian E.V.O. Dankwah, would stay until March 14 and visit the capital Abuja, the cities of Kano, Kaduna and Port Harcourt where it would meet government officials, human rights groups and individuals.

Government officials said the team would see detainees including presidential claimant Moshood Abiola and 19 youths from the Ogoni minority tribe who are detained over the 1994 murder of four Ogoni chiefs.

The Ogoni youths face the death penalty like executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa, who was hanged with eight other Ogoni minority rights activists in 1995 over the same murders after a trial condemned internationally as flawed.
